excerpt: Most of the AI papers I liked lately are about how AI fools the people using it. That is more useful to me than another agent with a Sharpe of 3. This is a new Friday list: the week’s research on data, AI and quant trading, with the links. The first one reaches back about three weeks. Crypto and market microstructure Path-Independent Deleveraging Rules (Schlegel and Mamageishvili) Which profitable positions should a perp venue close when liquidations cannot cover a bankrupt account? The authors narrow the fair rules to a one-parameter family. Replayed on Hyperliquid’s ADL of 10 October 2025, intermediate settings “significantly improve on the observed allocation”. Figure 3 in the paper. Right: each rule’s fairness against its risk 24 hours later; lower is better on both. The red square is what Hyperliquid did. Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book (Ramachandran) Market makers updating quotes over different lookback horizons give order flow power-law memory, and rough volatility follows. Six months of Binance data, about 790 million orders, fit the model. Figure 2 in the paper (CC BY-SA 4.0). Left: the Hurst parameter of order activity in BTC, ETH and SOL, spot and perps, per 30-day block. All sit far below the 1/2 of Brownian motion. Settlement Manipulation in Prediction Markets (Dai, Jia and Yu) Traders moved spot to settle Polymarket’s five-minute Bitcoin contract their way, mostly at retail’s expense. It stopped once settlement moved to a 60-second average price. The old FX fixing problem, on a five-minute clock. Figure 12 in the paper. Binance BTC spot through each five-minute cycle. The jump in order flow before the close (grey) flattens under the 60-second average price (orange). title: I Built IQ-Stream: Streaming LLM Tokens to the Browser Without the Workarounds
author: valerione
snippet: When I started working on streaming in Neuron AI, I thought it was the easy part of the framework. The model produces text, you forward it to the browser, the user watches the answer appear. Done. It took me months, a custom protocol, a TypeScript package, and a long look at a…
excerpt: When I started working on streaming in Neuron AI, I thought it was the easy part of the framework. The model produces text, you forward it to the browser, the user watches the answer appear. Done. It took me months, a custom protocol, a TypeScript package, and a long look at a pricing page to admit I was wrong. This article is the story of that journey and of the tool that came out of it. IQ-Stream is a streaming server that does one job: it carries the tokens generated by a large language model (LLM) from your application backend to your users’ browsers in real time, using Server-Sent Events. If a browser loses its connection in the middle of an answer, it gets back every event it missed as soon as it reconnects. Your backend talks to it with plain HTTP requests, so it works with PHP and with any other language. I’ll start from the basics, because many of you are building your first agent right now and not everything here is obvious. If you already know why streaming matters and how it works in PHP, feel free to skip ahead to the section about the limits I found along the way. What streaming means in an AI application An LLM doesn’t write an answer all at once. It generates text in small pieces called tokens, roughly a word or a part of a word each, one after another. A long answer of a few thousand tokens can take from tens of seconds to more than a minute to complete. If your application waits for the whole thing before showing anything, the user stares at a spinner for that entire time. Streaming means sending each piece to the browser as soon as the model produces it, so the user starts reading immediately. With agents, there’s more than text to stream. An agent can reason before answering, decide to call a tool (a PHP function that queries your database or calls an external API), wait for the result, and then continue writing. Users want to see all of this as it happens, otherwise a thirty second tool call looks like a frozen application. In Neuron AI you…

title: Carpool – cut LLM costs by batching tasks and compiling repeated calls into code
author: nmayp
snippet: If your script, pipeline or agent makes a separate model call for every item, each call pays for its fixed setup again: system prompt, tool schemas, instructions. carpool puts independent tasks in one request, checks every answer against the source it cites, and redoes only the…
excerpt: If your script, pipeline or agent makes a separate model call for every item, each call pays for its fixed setup again: system prompt, tool schemas, instructions. carpool puts independent tasks in one request, checks every answer against the source it cites, and redoes only the ones that fail. In our tests on Claude, that cut the cost per accepted answer by about 80% against one lean call per task, and by 93–96% against one Claude Code agent call per task, with no regressions.1 In Claude Code: claude plugin marketplace add nmayp/carpoolclaude plugin install carpool@carpool Or try the library offline, no API key needed: pip install carpool-agentscarpool bench carpool bench uses a mock model with a fixed cost per call, so it shows how carpool works rather than what it saves. For real numbers run carpool bench --backend claude-lean (or claude-code, codex, ollama:<model>, …). A lean call is Claude through Claude Code with no tools and a one-line system prompt (about 1,100 tokens of fixed setup); an agent call is a full Claude Code session (about 26,000). Repeat runs came out cheaper still because the provider cached the grouped prompt, so the table quotes first runs. Every raw JSON file, the ablation, the group-size sweep and the agent experiments are in docs/RESULTS.md. What we measured: - The saving comes from sharing the request. Shortening evidence with one call per task saved 2.5% on the ops tasks and cost 5.7% more on SQuAD. - The bigger each call's fixed setup is compared with one task's own text, the more carpool saves. On a small local model with almost no fixed setup, savings were 8–51% and grouping cost some quality. - A well-behaved interactive agent (Claude Code triaging 20 tickets) showed no measurable change, because it already reads everything in one go. When agents did spawn one subagent per file, it cost 4–6× more. The four rules: - Run exact work as code. Lookups, counts and filters don't need a model: in the original study, 1,000 of 1,000 order…

title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
author: Junrui Zhang, Zeyu Xu, Runchuan Zhu
snippet: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE)…
excerpt: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated (r=-0.5, ple 0.05) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
author: Byunggu Yu, Justin Kim
snippet: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural…
excerpt: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
author: Y. Lu, L. Wang, S. Okada
snippet: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain…
excerpt: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
author: Sandeep Dhuri
snippet: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one…
excerpt: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
snippet: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5 Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting…
excerpt: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5 Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work. With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos? I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result. Two goals I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API. For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines. How it works The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. title: LayoutRecall: Preserving Appearance in Multi-Round 3D Layout-Controlled Image Editing
author: Yankuan Chi, Xin Lin, Baihan Yang
snippet: 3D layout-controlled image editing gives users explicit control over object placement and camera viewpoint. In a sequence of edits, however, the latest image can lose the appearance of an object when it is occluded or leaves view. The target layout specifies where the object…
excerpt: 3D layout-controlled image editing gives users explicit control over object placement and camera viewpoint. In a sequence of edits, however, the latest image can lose the appearance of an object when it is occluded or leaves view. The target layout specifies where the object should reappear, while its appearance must be recovered from earlier observations. We introduce LayoutRecall, a multi-round editor that stores and reuses appearance in the local coordinate systems of 3D boxes. Box-Surface Latent Memory retains image latents on box faces and retrieves them along rays in the target view. Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning supplies the retrieved tokens to a FLUX.2 editor using target-view positions, shared box-local embeddings, and object-wise attention. A correspondence loss encourages the editor to attend to matching observations during denoising. We also introduce LayoutLoop, a multi-round 3D layout-controlled image editing benchmark with calibrated layouts and designed revisits. We conduct extensive experiments on LayoutLoop and real-scene data to verify the ability of our method. The project page is at
